value.overview: The Common Chlorospingus is a small, active forest songbird formerly grouped with tanagers and now placed among the New World sparrows. It is often encountered in noisy mixed-species flocks, moving through dense vegetation while searching for insects and fruit. The species has many regional forms across the mountains of the Americas. In Costa Rica it is a familiar bird of middle-elevation forests, especially on the Caribbean and Pacific mountain slopes.
value.classification: The Common Chlorospingus belongs to the order Passeriformes and family Passerellidae. Its scientific name is Chlorospingus flavopectus; older sources may call it a bush-tanager because of its former placement in the tanager family.
value.identification: This is a small, compact bird with an olive-green back, grayish head, pale underparts, and a yellow or yellowish throat and upper breast. Many forms show a conspicuous white spot behind the eye, although the exact pattern varies geographically. The bill is short and conical, and the wings and tail are relatively dark. In Costa Rica, it can be confused with the higher-elevation Sooty-capped Chlorospingus, but the Common Chlorospingus generally occupies lower and middle elevations and has a different head pattern.
value.rangeHabitat: The Common Chlorospingus ranges from Mexico through Central America and much of the Andes to Bolivia and northwestern Argentina. In Costa Rica it is widespread in suitable mountain habitat, including the Cordilleras of Guanacaste, Tilarán, Central, and Talamanca, where it is commonly found in middle-elevation forest. It uses humid montane forest, cloud forest margins, dense second growth, bushy clearings, forest edges, gardens, and other areas with abundant understory vegetation. It generally occurs below the main range of the Sooty-capped Chlorospingus.
value.migrationStatus: It is primarily resident in Costa Rica and throughout most of its range. Local or seasonal movements, including changes in elevation, may occur in response to food supply, weather, or breeding conditions, but it is not a regular long-distance migrant.
value.breeding: The species builds a small cup-shaped nest in dense vegetation, commonly in a shrub or low tree, where surrounding foliage provides cover. The female performs most or all of the incubation, while both adults feed the nestlings. Breeding dates vary across its broad range. In Costa Rica, nesting activity is associated mainly with the seasonal breeding period, but the exact timing can differ among elevations and regions. Detailed information is not available for every Costa Rican population.
value.dietFeeding: The Common Chlorospingus eats a mixed diet of small insects and other arthropods, berries, soft fruits, and some seeds. It searches actively through leaves, twigs, moss, epiphytes, and dense shrubs, often making short movements between nearby perches. Fruit and other plant foods are important at many times, while insects are especially valuable when adults are feeding growing young. It may visit fruiting plants and feeding stations near forested habitats.
value.behavior: This species is energetic and social, often traveling in pairs or joining mixed-species flocks with other small forest birds. Individuals usually forage in the understory and lower to middle levels of vegetation, frequently calling while moving through cover. It may appear restless and difficult to follow as it hops between branches and foliage. During the breeding season, pairs can become more territorial, while outside that period larger groups may form around concentrated food sources.

conservation.populationTrend: The species remains widespread and generally common, but a precise global population estimate and a clearly documented overall trend are not available in the accessible assessment information.
